THE CASE AGAINST JACOB ZUMA I

By: Este de Klerk | Delivery

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
Former President Jacob Zuma's day in court could be drawing nearer. Media reports indicates that the NPA prosecution team unanimously recommended that 18 charges of fraud and corruption dating back mo

Unique Selling Point:
Former President Jacob Zuma's day in court could be drawing nearer. Media reports indicates that the NPA prosecution team unanimously recommended that 18 charges of fraud and corruption dating back more than a decade be reinstated.
NPA boss, Shaun Abrahams on Monday, 26 March 2018, indicated that he has made a decision on whether or not Jacob Zuma should be prosecuted. Many are questioning his timing - a week after Zuma resigned as president and only two days before Abrahams' own appeal against a December 2017 Pretoria High Court ruling that said Abraham's appointment was invalid and unlawful and should be set aside - was heard in the Constitutional Court.
Abrahams announced that he will announce his decision on whether or not to prosecute Zuma by Thursday, 15 March - this depending on whether the Concourt gives judgment before then and depending what the outcome will be. There is a possibility that the Concourt may uphold the Pretoria High Court ruling that Abrahams' appointment was invalid and unlawful and should be set aside; and that former NPA head Mxolisi Nxasana should be reinstated in this position - or that an entirely new NPA boss should be appointed by President Cyril Ramaphosa all together.

Council for the Helen Suzman Foundation (HSF) argued that it would be improper for Abrahams to announce whether or not Zuma is going to be prosecuted. He argued that the question is not whether Abrahams is independent, it's about whether he is perceived to be independent.

The HSF points to Appeal Court ruling on Spy Tapes case, where judges questioned why NPA had tried to defend irrational decision to drop Zuma prosecution. High Court found Abrahams had aligned himself with Zuma legal strategies. And it criticized how he failed to act against Jiba.

Adv Geoff Budlender, who argued for the lobby group Council for the Advancement of the South African Constitution (Casac) argued that the question is not just whether to prosecute (Zuma), but who should prosecute? These decisions need to be made by a person in whom the public has confidence. There are too many senior people in the NPA who carry toxic baggage.
Justice Cachalia again asks Budlender if he realizes that not allowing Abrahams to announce his Zuma decision may delay the prosecution process by a year. Delay would be justified, Budlender says, nut he doubts it would take long for President Ramaphosa to appoint new NDPP.


Summary:
In April 2009, shortly before Jacob Zuma became the president of the country, then NPA boss, Mokotedi Mpshe announced that he was dropping the charges against Zuma. Since then, his decision has been the subject of one of the country's most drawn-out and longest-running legal battles. The DA relentlessly pursued Zuma and the NPA to make them reinstate the charges. The charges relate to the Arms Deal. The Pretoria High Court last year ruled that Mpshe was "reckless" in dropping the charges and this judgment was upheld by the SCA in Zuma and the NPA's appeal.

NPA boss Shaun Abrahams allowed Zuma an opportunity to hand in recommendations on why he should not be charged. At the end of February, City Press reported that the team of five senior prosecutors who studied former President Jacob Zuma's recommendations to avoid his day in court have recommended that all charges against him be reinstated.

Zuma is expected to face 18 charges of corruption, money laundering and racketeering, originating from 783 questionable payments he received.

Further information:
THE STORY:
In 2003, then NPA head Bulelani Ngcuka announded that there was a prima facie case of corruption against Zuma. Ngcuka declined to prosecute Zuma, who was then deputy-president, on the grounds that the state didn't have a winnable case. In a statement, Ngcuka said the decision was reached after what he considered to be one of the most difficult investigations that the NPA and "our young democracy" had witnessed.
"The investigating team recommended that we institute a criminal prosecution against [Zuma]... while there is a prima facie case of corruption against [Zuma], our prospects of success are not strong enough," he said.
"We cannot continue with a prolonged investigation that cast a shadow over [Zuma], whilst we are not assured of the outcome."
Two years later, in 2005, the NPA - then headed by Ngcuka's successor, advocate Vusi Pikoli, officially charged Zuma. This followed the conviction of Zuma's financial advisor and close friend, Schabir Shaik, on two charges of corruption, and for soliciting a bribe for Zuma from French arms deal beneficiary, Thales, in exchange for possible investigation into the arms deal. Schaik was sentenced to 15 years in prison. In his judgment on 2 June 2005, trial Judge Hillary Squires, described the relations between Zuma and Shaik as "mutually beneficial symbiosis".

Zuma previously only faced two charges of corruption based on the indictment in the Shaik trial. But 14 charges were then added including racketeering, fraud and money laundering.

It was alleged that Zuma personally met and interceded with Shaik's prospective business partners, mostly Thales, to try to secure Shaik's interests.

The essence of the racketeering charge was that Zuma, Thales and Shaik effectively formed an enterprise called Nkobi Investments that existed because of their alleged corrupt deeds.

Zuma's charge sheet disclosed that between 1995 and 2005, Zuma or his family allegedly received 783 payments totaling more than R4 million from Shaik or his companies.
The rest of the charges relate to Zuma's alleged non-declaration of benefits to Parliament and Cabinet and alleged tax evasion for not revealing his payments from Shaik to the South African Revenue Service.

In 2006, however, the Pietermaritzburg High Court dismissed Zuma's corruption case because the prosecution team was not ready to bring a case. In 2007, shortly after he was elected president of the ANC in Polokwane he was charged again. After a series of challenges by Zuma's legal team, the case was to be heard in August 2009. But before he could appear in court, then acting NPA head, Mokotedi Mpshe announced the charges against Zuma would be dropped because of alleged political interference leading to an abuse of the legal process. Mpshe's decision resulted from transcripts of telephone calls - dubbed the Spy Tapes - between former Scorpions boss, Leonard McCarthy, and Ngcuka. Mpshe said the transcripts revealed that McCarthy and Ngcuka colluded to change the timing of the announcement of the reinstitution of the charges against Zuma to damage his presidential campaign.

The DA relentlessly drove this case. And in 2016, the North Gauteng High Court found the decision to drop the charges against Zuma was illegal and irrational. The court set the decision aside, effectively reinstating the charges. Zuma and the NPA appealed the judgment in the SCA, but the SCA upheld the Pta High Court's ruling. NPA boss Shaun Abrahams gave Zuma until the end of January to file recommendations on why he shouldn't be prosecuted. And in the last week of February, Abrahams announced he is ready to make the announcement on whether or not Zuma should be charged.

It is possible that Zuma's legal team would have argued that too much time - 12 years - has passed between now and charges first being brought, for justice to be done. The may have also pointed to the fact that one key piece of evidence - a KPMG report into the financial relationship between Shaik and Zuma - was prepared by the same KPMG auditor responsible for the flawed report into the SARS "Rogue unit".

Hawks head Yolisa Matakata was quoted by City Press as saying that the evidence for the case remained intact and the witnesses have been located. It is reported that as many as 218 witnesses may be called by the state of the case proceeds in court.

The original 2007 indictment, signed off by director of special operations Aubrey Mngwengwe in December 2007, indicated Zuma was charged with 18 counts of corruption, fraud and racketeering. Zuma was accused number one, charged alongside French companies Thint Holding and Thint Pty - now known as Thales. It has been reported that the charges against Thales will be reinstated alongside Zuma if the case proceeds.

Daily Maverick's Rebecca Davis pulled the initial indictment out of her archives:

Name: Jacob Zuma, aka "Accused 1"
Then: In the period covered by the indictment, Zuma was initially MEC for Economic Affairs and Tourism in KwaZulu-Natal, and subsequently deputy president of the ANC. In the indictment, he stands accused of having received 783 bribe payments between 1995 and 2005 totalling R4,072,499.85. In exchange, Zuma is accused of having intervened to assist his benefactors in the arms deal. "Accused 1," records the indictment, "needed funds to pay for the development of his traditional residential village estate at Nkandla in rural northern KZN."
Now: Zuma resigned as president of the ANC and South Africa on 14 February 2018 after being recalled by the ANC. Since stepping down, Zuma has been seen at farewell functions at Tuynhuys and the Union Buildings.

Name: Pierre Jean-Marie Robert Moynot
Then: Moynot was a director of French arms company Thint (subsequently renamed Thales). Thint was the firm accused of paying bribes in order to secure the arms deal. The 2007 indictment accuses Moynot of brokering a meeting between Zuma and Thales to engage his support.
Now: Moynot has been maintaining a low profile for the last few years. A Linked-In profile, however, still lists a Pierre Moynot as working for Thales International in Johannesburg.

Name: Jean-Paul Perrier
Then: Perrier was the head of Thomson-CSF International, subsequently Thales International. In the indictment, he is accused of conspiring with Schabir Shaik to pay a bribe to Zuma of R500,000 per year.
Now: Perrier is currently listed as an adviser to the chairman of Thales. In July 2017, he was reported as being under investigation by French authorities as part of a case involving kickbacks on a Malaysian submarine deal in 2002.

Name: Yann Leo Renaud de Jomaron
Then: De Jomaron was the head of Thales International Africa. He was accused of conspiring with Perrier and Shaik to pay bribes to Zuma.
Now: De Jomaron's whereabouts are unclear. In 2007 he was known to have residency in Mauritius as well.

Name: Schabir Shaik
Then: Shaik was a Thales director and held shares in the arms company through his Nkobi Investments. He is accused of conspiring to bribe Zuma, and of acting as Zuma's financial adviser free of charge. In exchange, Zuma is alleged to have used "his powers as MEC and/or Deputy President of the ANC to further the private business interests of Shaik". Shaik is the only one of the gang to see the inside of a jail cell to date, having been sentenced in late 2006 to 15 years for fraud and corruption.
Now: Shaik was released on medical parole in March 2009 after his doctors informed the parole board that he was in the grip of a terminal illness and did not have long to live. Since his release, he has been spotted playing golf in apparently good health. He currently resides in Morningside, Durban.

Name: Alain Thetard
Then: Thetard was a Thales director, accused of conspiring to bribe Zuma. He met with Shaik, the indictment reads, in order for Shaik "to convey [Zuma's] request for a bribe to Thetard". At Shaik's corruption trial, an encrypted fax emerged in which Thetard recorded the terms of the R500,000 a year payment to Zuma. Thetard refused to testify in Shaik's trial.
Now: A Linked-in profile records one Alain Thetard as working for Thales in Germany.

Name: Chippy Shaik
Then: Brother of Schabir, Shamin "Chippy" Shaik, was chief of acquisitions in the department of defence at the time of the arms deal. He is not a major feature of the 2007 indictment. During February's informal arms deal tribunal, however, lawyer Ajay Sooklal claimed that Thales' Moynot paid $1-million to Chippy Shaik. In 2007, a German newspaper also claimed that Shaik had received a R21-million bribe from another defence company.
Now: In 2007 it was reported that Shaik was emigrating to Australia. In 2014 he gave evidence at the arms deal commission.

Name: Patricia de Lille
Then: De Lille appears in the 2007 indictment as a result of her whistle-blowing on the arms deal. It records how De Lille, then a PAC MP, "gave notice in Parliament that she wished to table a motion regarding alleged irregularities in the arms deal" on 9 September 1999. The motion, tabled a few weeks later, "received extensive publicity".
Now: The embattled Cape Town Mayor is herself fighting corruption charges brought against her by her party, the DA.

Press Release:


The Case against Zuma

After years of delays and obfuscation, it seems Jacob Zuma’s past is finally catching up with him. Armed with a docket of multiple counts of fraud and corruption, the National Prosecuting Authority believes it has a strong case against the former president. But could Zuma still have a few smart legal cards to play?

Producer: Este de Klerk

Presenter: Devi Sankaree Govender

Script:


THE CASE AGAINST JACOB ZUMA
PRODUCER: ESTE DE KLERK
PRESENTER: DEVI SANKAREE GOVENDER
EDITOR: FLORIS KOTZE
BROADCAST DATE: 25 MARCH 2018

VO: It's been more than a decade since former president Jacob Zuma was first served with an indictment on fraud, corruption, money laundering and racketeering charges.
Since Zuma was first charged in 2005, there have been significant markers in his political tenure: He was fired as deputy-president; then triumphed over Mbeki, becoming the ANC President; the charges were struck off the roll, then reinstated, then dropped again in 2009.
This undoubtedly paved a golden way for Zuma to become President in 2009.
And as President, he seemingly became untouchable… until now.
BANTU HOLOMISA: He was trying to blindfold the South Africans, but he cannot fool all of us. Today Zuma is a suspect.
MAVUSO MSIMANG: The ANC played a rather unfortunate roll in all of these things. They used their majority to act and protect a person who should have been given the opportunity to appear in court.
DEVI LINK: One month almost to the day after former President Jacob Zuma resigned, his appointee, National Director of Public Prosecutions Shaun Abrahams announced that Zuma will be prosecuted on corruption charges - the same charges which has dogged the President for the past 13 years.
VO: The charges all relate to the multi-billion rands arms deal and alleged bribes paid to Zuma.
He will face 16 charges: two of corruption; 12 of fraud; one of money laundering; and one of racketeering.
Zuma's original 2007 charge sheet disclosed that between 95 and 2002, Zuma or his family allegedly received 783 payments totaling more than R4 million from his former financial advisor, Schabir Shaik or his companies.
VUSI PIKOLI: The issue is that no one is above the law.
VO: Advocate Vusi Pikoli was the first NPA head to officially charge Zuma in 2005. He says the chances that Zuma would be convicted looks promising.
VUSI PIKOLI: If the matter were to proceed as envisaged, I don't see Mr Zuma being acquitted.
SHAUN ABRAHAMS/NPA NEWS CONFERENCE 16 MARCH 2018: We have a reasonable prospect of a successful prosecution.
VO: At a news conference last Friday, NPA boss, advocate Shaun Abrahams announced that Zuma's representations on why he should not be prosecuted were unsuccessful.
SHAUN ABRAHAMS/NPA NEWS CONFERENCE 16 MARCH 2018: Mr Zuma's representation, broadly speaking, largely relates to allegations of a prosecution characterised by prosecutorial manipulation, impropriety, fair trial abuses, prosecutorial misconduct, deliberate leaking of information to the media and irrational decisions made by various national directors and/or acting national directors of public prosecution.
DEVI LINK: Jacob Zuma has always maintained he wanted his day in court - that day is around the corner.
The reinstatement of the charges follows the Supreme Court of Appeal's ruling last year which dismissed Zuma and the NPA's appeal against the High Court judgment which declared invalid the decision by then NPA head Mokotedi Mpshe to drop the charges in 2009.
Mpshe's decision was taken on the grounds of a political conspiracy against Zuma. He based his finding on the so-called spy tapes -- recorded telephone conversations between Bulelani Ngcuka, former NPA head and then Scorpions boss, Leonard McCarthy.
The Democratic Alliance relentlessly pursued the case for eight years -- while Zuma, the NPA and Abrahams frustrated and opposed the case at every turn.
Questions were raised about the timing of Abrahams' announcement.
VUSI PIKOLI: Again those are the representations when nothing new, you know? what had changed in between? Is it because of the change of political leaders?
VO: As was the case in the past, the ANC has again vouched that the former president is innocent until proven guilty. But there are ANC veterans like Mavuso Msimang who believe that Zuma's been shielded for too long.
MAVUSO MSIMANG: in the end one said, you know, it's going to be very important for South Africans to know that what Jacob Zuma and his national executive colleagues are doing, does not represent the values of the African National Congress. It was very important that South Africans know that that's not how the ANC… that's the reason I and other people decided just to speak out. Somebody must know that the ANC is not what they are seeing.
VO: United Democratic Movement leader, Bantu Holomisa says it's not surprising that the ANC will support Zuma till the end.
BANTU HOLOMISA: The ANC has long been putting the interest of their leaders and itself ahead of the country. So, we are not surprised that they decided to defend Zuma. When people are saying there's new dawn and I always ask myself new dawn, said by the same group of people who were defending Zuma?
MAVUSO MSIMANG: former President ought to be saying guys I have not committed any crime and I'll prove that in court when I get the opportunity. But, with so much having been said against me, I… I want to clear my name first.

VO: But will he?
The mere reason that the charges have been reinstated, doesn't mean that Zuma sets foot in the dock within the next few weeks or months, says former Constitutional Court Justice Johann Kriegler.
JUSTICE JOHANN KRIEGLER: The possibilities for further delay are virtually infinite.
VO: With Zuma now in a tight corner, one can expect that his legal team will fight to keep him out of the dock, says criminal law expert, professor James Grant. The possible delays in the case may include .... Zuma taking Abrahams' decision to prosecute him on review.
PROF JAMES GRANT: In this case it would be saying that given the evidence and the facts before the particular person who made this decision, they could never have rationally arrived at this ultimate conclusion.
VUSI PIKOLI: He can only take the rejection of his representations on review. Which of course directly mean that he's challenging the reinstatement of charges.
VO: Over the last decade, Zuma has shown that he will use every legal means at his disposal to stay out of court. But even if Zuma takes the decision on review, it will not suspend the decision to prosecute.
MAVUSO MSIMANG: The last thing you want to see impugned is your honour. If he doesn't go to court the conclusion that people will draw is that he's afraid. He is guilty of what he has been charged on.
VO: Unfortunately, it's you and I who have to cough up for these delays.
DEVI LINK: The office of the State Attorney revealed that the State and therefore the taxpayers had already paid R15,3 million to fund Jacob Zuma's legal fees in connection with the Spy Tapes legal saga.
VO: The Opposition is livid after President Ramaphosa announced Zuma's future legal costs would be carried by the State, subject to him refunding the money if he's convicted.
PRESIDENT CYRIL RAMAPHOSA IN PARLIAMENT: This stems from a request by the former president which he made in 2006 for legal representation at state expense in respect of the criminal proceedings.
BANTU HOLOMISA: Well, this is where we would be raising our hand once more as opposition parties to challenge that if Cyril Ramaposa's agreement which we don't even know, he would allow Zuma to use state resources. He can take it to the review if he has money, but not at the expense of our… of us as South Africans.
VO: The DA said it will approach the court to seek a declaratory order that payment of all the legal fees for the case are declared unlawful.
JUSTICE JOHANN KRIEGLER: Up until now apparently, Mr Zuma's legal fees had been paid by you and me and the other tax payers. There is a strong suggestion that that regime is to be changed. If, in future, Mr Zuma has to pay it for his own fees, pay his own costs from his own pocket, it would be a very much more difficult exercise than merely tapping into the public purse to pay his fees and that may be a disincentive.
PROF JAMES GRANT: You're talking probably in the end something in the order of about 30 to 50 million, I expect.
VO: A hefty bill by all counts - but with more than 200 on the State's witness list, it will be a drawn-out case.
DEVI: What will the State have to proof?
PROF JAMES GRANT: The state will have to prove every element of all of the crimes. The main crime here though is corruption. Corruption is effectively about an improper benefit for an improper influence. So it's improper in, improper out. And there has to be both of those and it has to be intentional. Now, the intentional part is where I expect Jacob Zuma is going to place the emphasis in his defence.
VO: Another factor that Zuma's defence may raise -- even before the trial -- is the credibility of one key piece of evidence: a KPMG report into the financial relationship between Schabir Shaik and Jacob Zuma. This report was prepared by the same KPMG auditor responsible for the flawed report into the SARS "rogue unit" -- But the report was accepted as evidence by Judge Hilary Squires during the Shaik trial.
With the infinite possibilities of delays, Justice Kriegler believes that there is a slight chance of Zuma actually never being tried.
RETIRED CONCOURT JUSTICE JOHANN KRIEGLER: He's not a child. He's lifespan is limited and the lifespan of the court case forward before it actually starts, is virtually unlimited.
VO: There's no doubt that the trial will be protracted, but the wheels of justice have slowly started to turn.

PROMOS

PROMO 1: 15"

The wheels of justice have slowly started to turn. But will former president Jacob Zuma inevitably stand trial?
JUDGE KRIEGLER: there's a possibility of Mr Zuma never actually being tried, yes.

PROMO 2: 15"

It seems Jacob Zuma's past is finally catching up with him, as the NPA will soon be heading to court. But what are their chances of a successful prosecution?
VUSI PIKOLI: If the matter were to proceed as envisaged, I don't see Mr Zuma being acquitted.

PROMO 3: 10"
Jacob Zuma's day in court could be drawing close as he faces charges of fraud and corruption. Opposition parties consider it a victory, but will he get his day in court?

At the end of February, City Press reported that the team of five senior prosecutors who studied former President Jacob Zuma's recommendations to avoid his day in court have recommended that all charges against him be reinstated. Zuma is expected to face 18 charges of corruption, money laundering and racketeering, originating from 783 questionable payments he received. Further information: THE STORY: In 2003, then NPA head Bulelani Ngcuka announded that there was a prima facie case of corruption against Zuma. Ngcuka declined to prosecute Zuma, who was then deputy-president, on the grounds that the state didn't have a winnable case. In a statement, Ngcuka said the decision was reached after what he considered to be one of the most difficult investigations that the NPA and "our young democracy" had witnessed. "The investigating team recommended that we institute a criminal prosecution against [Zuma]... while there is a prima facie case of corruption against [Zuma], our prospects of success are not strong enough," he said. "We cannot continue with a prolonged investigation that cast a shadow over [Zuma], whilst we are not assured of the outcome." Two years later, in 2005, the NPA - then headed by Ngcuka's successor, advocate Vusi Pikoli, officially charged Zuma. This followed the conviction of Zuma's financial advisor and close friend, Schabir Shaik, on two charges of corruption, and for soliciting a bribe for Zuma from French arms deal beneficiary, Thales, in exchange for possible investigation into the arms deal. Schaik was sentenced to 15 years in prison. In his judgment on 2 June 2005, trial Judge Hillary Squires, described the relations between Zuma and Shaik as "mutually beneficial symbiosis". Zuma previously only faced two charges of corruption based on the indictment in the Shaik trial. But 14 charges were then added including racketeering, fraud and money laundering. It was alleged that Zuma personally met and interceded with Shaik's prospective business partners, mostly Thales, to try to secure Shaik's interests. The essence of the racketeering charge was that Zuma, Thales and Shaik effectively formed an enterprise called Nkobi Investments that existed because of their alleged corrupt deeds. Zuma's charge sheet disclosed that between 1995 and 2005, Zuma or his family allegedly received 783 payments totaling more than R4 million from Shaik or his companies. The rest of the charges relate to Zuma's alleged non-declaration of benefits to Parliament and Cabinet and alleged tax evasion for not revealing his payments from Shaik to the South African Revenue Service. In 2006, however, the Pietermaritzburg High Court dismissed Zuma's corruption case because the prosecution team was not ready to bring a case. In 2007, shortly after he was elected president of the ANC in Polokwane he was charged again. After a series of challenges by Zuma's legal team, the case was to be heard in August 2009. But before he could appear in court, then acting NPA head, Mokotedi Mpshe announced the charges against Zuma would be dropped because of alleged political interference leading to an abuse of the legal process. Mpshe's decision resulted from transcripts of telephone calls - dubbed the Spy Tapes - between former Scorpions boss, Leonard McCarthy, and Ngcuka. Mpshe said the transcripts revealed that McCarthy and Ngcuka colluded to change the timing of the announcement of the reinstitution of the charges against Zuma to damage his presidential campaign. The DA relentlessly drove this case. And in 2016, the North Gauteng High Court found the decision to drop the charges against Zuma was illegal and irrational. The court set the decision aside, effectively reinstating the charges. Zuma and the NPA appealed the judgment in the SCA, but the SCA upheld the Pta High Court's ruling. NPA boss Shaun Abrahams gave Zuma until the end of January to file recommendations on why he shouldn't be prosecuted. And in the last week of February, Abrahams announced he is ready to make the announcement on whether or not Zuma should be charged. It is possible that Zuma's legal team would have argued that too much time - 12 years - has passed between now and charges first being brought, for justice to be done. The may have also pointed to the fact that one key piece of evidence - a KPMG report into the financial relationship between Shaik and Zuma - was prepared by the same KPMG auditor responsible for the flawed report into the SARS "Rogue unit". Hawks head Yolisa Matakata was quoted by City Press as saying that the evidence for the case remained intact and the witnesses have been located. It is reported that as many as 218 witnesses may be called by the state of the case proceeds in court. The original 2007 indictment, signed off by director of special operations Aubrey Mngwengwe in December 2007, indicated Zuma was charged with 18 counts of corruption, fraud and racketeering. Zuma was accused number one, charged alongside French companies Thint Holding and Thint Pty - now known as Thales. It has been reported that the charges against Thales will be reinstated alongside Zuma if the case proceeds. Daily Maverick's Rebecca Davis pulled the initial indictment out of her archives: Name: Jacob Zuma, aka "Accused 1" Then: In the period covered by the indictment, Zuma was initially MEC for Economic Affairs and Tourism in KwaZulu-Natal, and subsequently deputy president of the ANC. In the indictment, he stands accused of having received 783 bribe payments between 1995 and 2005 totalling R4,072,499.85. In exchange, Zuma is accused of having intervened to assist his benefactors in the arms deal. "Accused 1," records the indictment, "needed funds to pay for the development of his traditional residential village estate at Nkandla in rural northern KZN." Now: Zuma resigned as president of the ANC and South Africa on 14 February 2018 after being recalled by the ANC. Since stepping down, Zuma has been seen at farewell functions at Tuynhuys and the Union Buildings. Name: Pierre Jean-Marie Robert Moynot Then: Moynot was a director of French arms company Thint (subsequently renamed Thales). Thint was the firm accused of paying bribes in order to secure the arms deal. The 2007 indictment accuses Moynot of brokering a meeting between Zuma and Thales to engage his support. Now: Moynot has been maintaining a low profile for the last few years. A Linked-In profile, however, still lists a Pierre Moynot as working for Thales International in Johannesburg. Name: Jean-Paul Perrier Then: Perrier was the head of Thomson-CSF International, subsequently Thales International. In the indictment, he is accused of conspiring with Schabir Shaik to pay a bribe to Zuma of R500,000 per year. Now: Perrier is currently listed as an adviser to the chairman of Thales. In July 2017, he was reported as being under investigation by French authorities as part of a case involving kickbacks on a Malaysian submarine deal in 2002. Name: Yann Leo Renaud de Jomaron Then: De Jomaron was the head of Thales International Africa. He was accused of conspiring with Perrier and Shaik to pay bribes to Zuma. Now: De Jomaron's whereabouts are unclear. In 2007 he was known to have residency in Mauritius as well. Name: Schabir Shaik Then: Shaik was a Thales director and held shares in the arms company through his Nkobi Investments. He is accused of conspiring to bribe Zuma, and of acting as Zuma's financial adviser free of charge. In exchange, Zuma is alleged to have used "his powers as MEC and/or Deputy President of the ANC to further the private business interests of Shaik". Shaik is the only one of the gang to see the inside of a jail cell to date, having been sentenced in late 2006 to 15 years for fraud and corruption. Now: Shaik was released on medical parole in March 2009 after his doctors informed the parole board that he was in the grip of a terminal illness and did not have long to live. Since his release, he has been spotted playing golf in apparently good health. He currently resides in Morningside, Durban. Name: Alain Thetard Then: Thetard was a Thales director, accused of conspiring to bribe Zuma. He met with Shaik, the indictment reads, in order for Shaik "to convey [Zuma's] request for a bribe to Thetard". At Shaik's corruption trial, an encrypted fax emerged in which Thetard recorded the terms of the R500,000 a year payment to Zuma. Thetard refused to testify in Shaik's trial. Now: A Linked-in profile records one Alain Thetard as working for Thales in Germany. Name: Chippy Shaik Then: Brother of Schabir, Shamin "Chippy" Shaik, was chief of acquisitions in the department of defence at the time of the arms deal. He is not a major feature of the 2007 indictment. During February's informal arms deal tribunal, however, lawyer Ajay Sooklal claimed that Thales' Moynot paid $1-million to Chippy Shaik. In 2007, a German newspaper also claimed that Shaik had received a R21-million bribe from another defence company. Now: In 2007 it was reported that Shaik was emigrating to Australia. In 2014 he gave evidence at the arms deal commission. Name: Patricia de Lille Then: De Lille appears in the 2007 indictment as a result of her whistle-blowing on the arms deal. It records how De Lille, then a PAC MP, "gave notice in Parliament that she wished to table a motion regarding alleged irregularities in the arms deal" on 9 September 1999. The motion, tabled a few weeks later, "received extensive publicity". Now: The embattled Cape Town Mayor is herself fighting corruption charges brought against her by her party, the DA. Vrahimis 05 April 2018 Press Release: The Case against Zuma After years of delays and obfuscation, it seems Jacob Zuma’s past is finally catching up with him. Armed with a docket of multiple counts of fraud and corruption, the National Prosecuting Authority believes it has a strong case against the former president. But could Zuma still have a few smart legal cards to play? Producer: Este de Klerk Presenter: Devi Sankaree Govender Script: THE CASE AGAINST JACOB ZUMA PRODUCER: ESTE DE KLERK PRESENTER: DEVI SANKAREE GOVENDER EDITOR: FLORIS KOTZE BROADCAST DATE: 25 MARCH 2018 VO: It's been more than a decade since former president Jacob Zuma was first served with an indictment on fraud, corruption, money laundering and racketeering charges. Since Zuma was first charged in 2005, there have been significant markers in his political tenure: He was fired as deputy-president; then triumphed over Mbeki, becoming the ANC President; the charges were struck off the roll, then reinstated, then dropped again in 2009. This undoubtedly paved a golden way for Zuma to become President in 2009. And as President, he seemingly became untouchable… until now. BANTU HOLOMISA: He was trying to blindfold the South Africans, but he cannot fool all of us. Today Zuma is a suspect. MAVUSO MSIMANG: The ANC played a rather unfortunate roll in all of these things. They used their majority to act and protect a person who should have been given the opportunity to appear in court. DEVI LINK: One month almost to the day after former President Jacob Zuma resigned, his appointee, National Director of Public Prosecutions Shaun Abrahams announced that Zuma will be prosecuted on corruption charges - the same charges which has dogged the President for the past 13 years. VO: The charges all relate to the multi-billion rands arms deal and alleged bribes paid to Zuma. He will face 16 charges: two of corruption; 12 of fraud; one of money laundering; and one of racketeering. Zuma's original 2007 charge sheet disclosed that between 95 and 2002, Zuma or his family allegedly received 783 payments totaling more than R4 million from his former financial advisor, Schabir Shaik or his companies. VUSI PIKOLI: The issue is that no one is above the law. VO: Advocate Vusi Pikoli was the first NPA head to officially charge Zuma in 2005. He says the chances that Zuma would be convicted looks promising. VUSI PIKOLI: If the matter were to proceed as envisaged, I don't see Mr Zuma being acquitted. SHAUN ABRAHAMS/NPA NEWS CONFERENCE 16 MARCH 2018: We have a reasonable prospect of a successful prosecution. VO: At a news conference last Friday, NPA boss, advocate Shaun Abrahams announced that Zuma's representations on why he should not be prosecuted were unsuccessful. SHAUN ABRAHAMS/NPA NEWS CONFERENCE 16 MARCH 2018: Mr Zuma's representation, broadly speaking, largely relates to allegations of a prosecution characterised by prosecutorial manipulation, impropriety, fair trial abuses, prosecutorial misconduct, deliberate leaking of information to the media and irrational decisions made by various national directors and/or acting national directors of public prosecution. DEVI LINK: Jacob Zuma has always maintained he wanted his day in court - that day is around the corner. The reinstatement of the charges follows the Supreme Court of Appeal's ruling last year which dismissed Zuma and the NPA's appeal against the High Court judgment which declared invalid the decision by then NPA head Mokotedi Mpshe to drop the charges in 2009. Mpshe's decision was taken on the grounds of a political conspiracy against Zuma. He based his finding on the so-called spy tapes -- recorded telephone conversations between Bulelani Ngcuka, former NPA head and then Scorpions boss, Leonard McCarthy. The Democratic Alliance relentlessly pursued the case for eight years -- while Zuma, the NPA and Abrahams frustrated and opposed the case at every turn. Questions were raised about the timing of Abrahams' announcement. VUSI PIKOLI: Again those are the representations when nothing new, you know? what had changed in between? Is it because of the change of political leaders? VO: As was the case in the past, the ANC has again vouched that the former president is innocent until proven guilty. But there are ANC veterans like Mavuso Msimang who believe that Zuma's been shielded for too long. MAVUSO MSIMANG: in the end one said, you know, it's going to be very important for South Africans to know that what Jacob Zuma and his national executive colleagues are doing, does not represent the values of the African National Congress. It was very important that South Africans know that that's not how the ANC… that's the reason I and other people decided just to speak out. Somebody must know that the ANC is not what they are seeing. VO: United Democratic Movement leader, Bantu Holomisa says it's not surprising that the ANC will support Zuma till the end. BANTU HOLOMISA: The ANC has long been putting the interest of their leaders and itself ahead of the country. So, we are not surprised that they decided to defend Zuma. When people are saying there's new dawn and I always ask myself new dawn, said by the same group of people who were defending Zuma? MAVUSO MSIMANG: former President ought to be saying guys I have not committed any crime and I'll prove that in court when I get the opportunity. But, with so much having been said against me, I… I want to clear my name first. VO: But will he? The mere reason that the charges have been reinstated, doesn't mean that Zuma sets foot in the dock within the next few weeks or months, says former Constitutional Court Justice Johann Kriegler. JUSTICE JOHANN KRIEGLER: The possibilities for further delay are virtually infinite. VO: With Zuma now in a tight corner, one can expect that his legal team will fight to keep him out of the dock, says criminal law expert, professor James Grant. The possible delays in the case may include .... Zuma taking Abrahams' decision to prosecute him on review. PROF JAMES GRANT: In this case it would be saying that given the evidence and the facts before the particular person who made this decision, they could never have rationally arrived at this ultimate conclusion. VUSI PIKOLI: He can only take the rejection of his representations on review. Which of course directly mean that he's challenging the reinstatement of charges. VO: Over the last decade, Zuma has shown that he will use every legal means at his disposal to stay out of court. But even if Zuma takes the decision on review, it will not suspend the decision to prosecute. MAVUSO MSIMANG: The last thing you want to see impugned is your honour. If he doesn't go to court the conclusion that people will draw is that he's afraid. He is guilty of what he has been charged on. VO: Unfortunately, it's you and I who have to cough up for these delays. DEVI LINK: The office of the State Attorney revealed that the State and therefore the taxpayers had already paid R15,3 million to fund Jacob Zuma's legal fees in connection with the Spy Tapes legal saga. VO: The Opposition is livid after President Ramaphosa announced Zuma's future legal costs would be carried by the State, subject to him refunding the money if he's convicted. PRESIDENT CYRIL RAMAPHOSA IN PARLIAMENT: This stems from a request by the former president which he made in 2006 for legal representation at state expense in respect of the criminal proceedings. BANTU HOLOMISA: Well, this is where we would be raising our hand once more as opposition parties to challenge that if Cyril Ramaposa's agreement which we don't even know, he would allow Zuma to use state resources. He can take it to the review if he has money, but not at the expense of our… of us as South Africans. VO: The DA said it will approach the court to seek a declaratory order that payment of all the legal fees for the case are declared unlawful. JUSTICE JOHANN KRIEGLER: Up until now apparently, Mr Zuma's legal fees had been paid by you and me and the other tax payers. There is a strong suggestion that that regime is to be changed. If, in future, Mr Zuma has to pay it for his own fees, pay his own costs from his own pocket, it would be a very much more difficult exercise than merely tapping into the public purse to pay his fees and that may be a disincentive. PROF JAMES GRANT: You're talking probably in the end something in the order of about 30 to 50 million, I expect. VO: A hefty bill by all counts - but with more than 200 on the State's witness list, it will be a drawn-out case. DEVI: What will the State have to proof? PROF JAMES GRANT: The state will have to prove every element of all of the crimes. The main crime here though is corruption. Corruption is effectively about an improper benefit for an improper influence. So it's improper in, improper out. And there has to be both of those and it has to be intentional. Now, the intentional part is where I expect Jacob Zuma is going to place the emphasis in his defence. VO: Another factor that Zuma's defence may raise -- even before the trial -- is the credibility of one key piece of evidence: a KPMG report into the financial relationship between Schabir Shaik and Jacob Zuma. This report was prepared by the same KPMG auditor responsible for the flawed report into the SARS "rogue unit" -- But the report was accepted as evidence by Judge Hilary Squires during the Shaik trial. With the infinite possibilities of delays, Justice Kriegler believes that there is a slight chance of Zuma actually never being tried. RETIRED CONCOURT JUSTICE JOHANN KRIEGLER: He's not a child. He's lifespan is limited and the lifespan of the court case forward before it actually starts, is virtually unlimited. VO: There's no doubt that the trial will be protracted, but the wheels of justice have slowly started to turn. PROMOS PROMO 1: 15" The wheels of justice have slowly started to turn. But will former president Jacob Zuma inevitably stand trial? JUDGE KRIEGLER: there's a possibility of Mr Zuma never actually being tried, yes. PROMO 2: 15" It seems Jacob Zuma's past is finally catching up with him, as the NPA will soon be heading to court. But what are their chances of a successful prosecution? VUSI PIKOLI: If the matter were to proceed as envisaged, I don't see Mr Zuma being acquitted. PROMO 3: 10" Jacob Zuma's day in court could be drawing close as he faces charges of fraud and corruption. Opposition parties consider it a victory, but will he get his day in court?

metadata.Unique Selling Point: Former President Jacob Zuma's day in court could be drawing nearer. Media reports indicates that the NPA prosecution team unanimously recommended that 18 charges of fraud and corruption dating back more than a decade be reinstated. NPA boss, Shaun Abrahams on Monday, 26 March 2018, indicated that he has made a decision on whether or not Jacob Zuma should be prosecuted. Many are questioning his timing - a week after Zuma resigned as president and only two days before Abrahams' own appeal against a December 2017 Pretoria High Court ruling that said Abraham's appointment was invalid and unlawful and should be set aside - was heard in the Constitutional Court. Abrahams announced that he will announce his decision on whether or not to prosecute Zuma by Thursday, 15 March - this depending on whether the Concourt gives judgment before then and depending what the outcome will be. There is a possibility that the Concourt may uphold the Pretoria High Court ruling that Abrahams' appointment was invalid and unlawful and should be set aside; and that former NPA head Mxolisi Nxasana should be reinstated in this position - or that an entirely new NPA boss should be appointed by President Cyril Ramaphosa all together. Council for the Helen Suzman Foundation (HSF) argued that it would be improper for Abrahams to announce whether or not Zuma is going to be prosecuted. He argued that the question is not whether Abrahams is independent, it's about whether he is perceived to be independent. The HSF points to Appeal Court ruling on Spy Tapes case, where judges questioned why NPA had tried to defend irrational decision to drop Zuma prosecution. High Court found Abrahams had aligned himself with Zuma legal strategies. And it criticized how he failed to act against Jiba. Adv Geoff Budlender, who argued for the lobby group Council for the Advancement of the South African Constitution (Casac) argued that the question is not just whether to prosecute (Zuma), but who should prosecute? These decisions need to be made by a person in whom the public has confidence. There are too many senior people in the NPA who carry toxic baggage. Justice Cachalia again asks Budlender if he realizes that not allowing Abrahams to announce his Zuma decision may delay the prosecution process by a year. Delay would be justified, Budlender says, nut he doubts it would take long for President Ramaphosa to appoint new NDPP.

In the indictment, he stands accused of having received 783 bribe payments between 1995 and 2005 totalling R4,072,499.85. In exchange, Zuma is accused of having intervened to assist his benefactors in the arms deal. "Accused 1," records the indictment, "needed funds to pay for the development of his traditional residential village estate at Nkandla in rural northern KZN." Now: Zuma resigned as president of the ANC and South Africa on 14 February 2018 after being recalled by the ANC. Since stepping down, Zuma has been seen at farewell functions at Tuynhuys and the Union Buildings. Name: Pierre Jean-Marie Robert Moynot Then: Moynot was a director of French arms company Thint (subsequently renamed Thales). Thint was the firm accused of paying bribes in order to secure the arms deal. The 2007 indictment accuses Moynot of brokering a meeting between Zuma and Thales to engage his support. Now: Moynot has been maintaining a low profile for the last few years. A Linked-In profile, however, still lists a Pierre Moynot as working for Thales International in Johannesburg. Name: Jean-Paul Perrier Then: Perrier was the head of Thomson-CSF International, subsequently Thales International. In the indictment, he is accused of conspiring with Schabir Shaik to pay a bribe to Zuma of R500,000 per year. Now: Perrier is currently listed as an adviser to the chairman of Thales. In July 2017, he was reported as being under investigation by French authorities as part of a case involving kickbacks on a Malaysian submarine deal in 2002. Name: Yann Leo Renaud de Jomaron Then: De Jomaron was the head of Thales International Africa. He was accused of conspiring with Perrier and Shaik to pay bribes to Zuma. Now: De Jomaron's whereabouts are unclear. In 2007 he was known to have residency in Mauritius as well. Name: Schabir Shaik Then: Shaik was a Thales director and held shares in the arms company through his Nkobi Investments. He is accused of conspiring to bribe Zuma, and of acting as Zuma's financial adviser free of charge. In exchange, Zuma is alleged to have used "his powers as MEC and/or Deputy President of the ANC to further the private business interests of Shaik". Shaik is the only one of the gang to see the inside of a jail cell to date, having been sentenced in late 2006 to 15 years for fraud and corruption. Now: Shaik was released on medical parole in March 2009 after his doctors informed the parole board that he was in the grip of a terminal illness and did not have long to live. Since his release, he has been spotted playing golf in apparently good health. He currently resides in Morningside, Durban. Name: Alain Thetard Then: Thetard was a Thales director, accused of conspiring to bribe Zuma. He met with Shaik, the indictment reads, in order for Shaik "to convey [Zuma's] request for a bribe to Thetard". At Shaik's corruption trial, an encrypted fax emerged in which Thetard recorded the terms of the R500,000 a year payment to Zuma. Thetard refused to testify in Shaik's trial. Now: A Linked-in profile records one Alain Thetard as working for Thales in Germany. Name: Chippy Shaik Then: Brother of Schabir, Shamin "Chippy" Shaik, was chief of acquisitions in the department of defence at the time of the arms deal. He is not a major feature of the 2007 indictment. During February's informal arms deal tribunal, however, lawyer Ajay Sooklal claimed that Thales' Moynot paid $1-million to Chippy Shaik. In 2007, a German newspaper also claimed that Shaik had received a R21-million bribe from another defence company. Now: In 2007 it was reported that Shaik was emigrating to Australia. In 2014 he gave evidence at the arms deal commission. Name: Patricia de Lille Then: De Lille appears in the 2007 indictment as a result of her whistle-blowing on the arms deal. It records how De Lille, then a PAC MP, "gave notice in Parliament that she wished to table a motion regarding alleged irregularities in the arms deal" on 9 September 1999. The motion, tabled a few weeks later, "received extensive publicity". Now: The embattled Cape Town Mayor is herself fighting corruption charges brought against her by her party, the DA.
